title: Certification of the genuine resolution of photon number resolving detectors
authors: Jef Pauwels, Towsif Taher, Roope Uola, Boris Korzh, Nicolas Brunner, Pavel Sekatski
abstract: Photon-number-resolving (PNR) detectors are essential components of photonic quantum technologies, yet thus far, no practical metric exists to certify how many photons they can genuinely resolve in a single measurement. Here we introduce an operational framework for quantifying the capability of a PNR detector to distinguish between different numbers of photons, i.e. its genuine resolution. In turn, we develop a practical and scalable protocol for certifying the genuine resolution of a detector, which is based on coherent state probes. We apply the method to a 28-pixel photon-number-resolving superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (PNR-SNSPD) and certify genuine four-outcome resolution. Our work highlights the critical requirements in terms of detector efficiency towards achieving high genuine resolution. This approach provides an operational benchmark for PNR detectors and fills a crucial gap in the characterization of photonic quantum devices.
summary: This paper introduces an operational framework to certify the genuine photon-number resolving capability of PNR detectors. By employing a 'guessing game' protocol with coherent state probes, the authors developed a scalable method to quantify detector performance without full tomography. They successfully applied this to test a superconducting nanowire detector, establishing critical benchmarks for efficiency and resolution.
main_problem: The primary challenge is establishing a practical, operational metric to certify the genuine resolution (the ability to distinguish between different photon numbers) of Photon-Number-Resolving (PNR) detectors.
main_result: The authors developed a scalable protocol using coherent state probes that successfully certified genuine four-outcome resolution for a tested PNR-SNSPD, while also quantifying the critical dependence of this resolution on detector efficiency.
method: They introduced an operational framework based on quantum measurement theory and utilized a 'guessing game' protocol involving weak coherent states to derive lower bounds on the genuine resolution by comparing measured guessing probabilities against theoretical witness inequalities.
model_or_system: The work focuses on characterizing PNR detectors, specifically testing a 28-pixel superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (PNR-SNSPD). The analysis is framed within the context of efficiency-limited quantum channels acting on Fock states.
key_observables: Genuine Resolution ($R$), Guessing Probability ($P_{	ext{guess}}$), Effective Efficiency ($\eta^*_m$), and statistical significance ($Z$).
important_parameters: Detector efficiency ($\eta$), the maximum photon number subspace limit ($m$), and the intensity bound ($I$) used in untrusted source models.
main_assumptions: The protocol avoids full measurement tomography by relying only on measurable input-output statistics from coherent probes; statistical analysis uses conservative bounds like Azuma–Hoeffding inequality.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual framework of quantifying photon counting ability, show data acquisition workflows using oscilloscope traces and histogram analysis, and present tables summarizing threshold efficiencies ($\eta_{	ext{th}}$) and certified effective efficiencies ($\eta^*_m$) for various subspaces ($m$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the theoretical gap (lack of certification metric) to proposing an operational framework using coherent state probes. It then details the mathematical derivation of witness inequalities, presents experimental data analysis comparing measured $P_{	ext{guess}}$ against trusted/untrusted bounds, and concludes by reporting certified resolution levels and effective efficiencies.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, scalable diagnostic tool for characterizing fundamental quantum hardware components (PNR detectors) that are crucial building blocks for quantum communication and computation protocols.

(a) In the 0-1 photon subspace (m=1), a maximal genuine resolution of R = 2 is certified. A genuine resolution R ≥3 is certified in the subspace with up to m = 3 photons; note that, with our data, this is not possible for m = 2. FIG. 4. Experimental setup for data acquisition. Coher- ent states are generated by a 1550 nm pulsed laser driven by an arbitrary waveform generator (AWG). The state intensities are controlled via variable optical attenuators (VOAs) and monitored using a 99:1 beam splitter and a power meter. The attenuated pulses probe a 28-pixel PNR-SNSPD operating at 0.8 K. The detector’s output signal, which encodes the number of firing pixels, is amplified both cryogenically (40 K) and at room temperature using low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) before being digitized on a high-resolution oscilloscope. A time-to-digital converter (TDC) measures the total number of laser pulses.
